title: Naranjo Algorithm
file: Naranjo Algorithm, one-page questionnaire (Canvas: adverse drug events module)
lecture: Wed 10/28 (Adverse Drug Events): introduced as a tool to determine causality of adverse drug reactions; after the break she had the class pull it up from Canvas, look at the 10 questions for timing, and went through the scoring and the time-related questions.
about: The Naranjo Algorithm is a one-page, ten-question scoring sheet that a clinician fills in to judge how likely it is that a particular drug caused a patient's adverse reaction. It matters for Exam 4 because Dr. Smith's study list says 'Be able to use the Naranjo algorithm': answer each question Yes, No or Do not know, add the points, and read off the band (definite, probable, possible or doubtful). The page's instruction reads 'To assess the adverse drug reaction, please answer the following questionnaire and give the pertinent score', and every 'Do not know' answer scores 0. The questions cover previous conclusive reports, whether the event appeared after the drug, improvement on discontinuation or with a specific antagonist, reappearance on re-administration, alternative causes or drugs, reappearance with a placebo, toxic drug concentrations, dose-related severity, a similar reaction on previous exposure, and confirmation by objective evidence. Points range from +2 to -1 per answer: questions 2 and 4 give +2 for Yes and -1 for No, questions 5 and 6 give -1 for Yes and +2 or +1 for No, and the rest give +1 for Yes and 0 for No. The total is categorized as 9 = definite, 5-8 = probable, 1-4 = possible, 0 = doubtful.

read_for: 1. The instruction line and the three answer columns: answer every question Yes, No or Do not know and write the points in the Score column; Do not know is 0 on all ten questions.
2. Question 1, Are there previous conclusive reports on this reaction? Yes +1, No 0, Do not know 0. Answered from the literature; she said to do your due diligence and dive into the literature.
3. Question 2, Did the adverse event appear after the suspected drug was administered? Yes +2, No -1, Do not know 0. A timing question she named.
4. Question 3, Did the adverse reaction improve when the drug was discontinued or a specific antagonist was administered? Yes +1, No 0, Do not know 0. A timing question she named.
5. Question 4, Did the adverse reaction reappear when the drug was re-administered? Yes +2, No -1, Do not know 0. A timing question she named ('definitely time').

6. Question 5, Are there alternative causes/drugs that could on their own have caused the reaction? Yes -1, No +2, Do not know 0. The scoring is reversed because another explanation points away from the drug.
7. Question 6, Did the reaction reappear when a placebo was given? Yes -1, No +1, Do not know 0. She counts it as time-related.

8. Questions 7 to 10, each Yes +1, No 0, Do not know 0: 7, was the drug detected in the blood or other fluids in concentrations known to be toxic; 8, was the reaction more severe when the dose was increased, or less severe when the dose was decreased; 9, did the patient have a similar reaction to the same or similar drugs in any previous exposure; 10, was the adverse event confirmed by any objective evidence.
9. The Total Score bands: 9 = definite; 5-8 = probable; 1-4 = possible; 0 = doubtful. She named the bands definite, probable, possible or remote; the page prints 'doubtful' for 0.

10. Scoring in practice: the four answers that lose a point are No on question 2, No on question 4, Yes on question 5 and Yes on question 6; the two +2 answers are Yes on questions 2 and 4 (and No on question 5). Totals can exceed 9 or fall below 0, for which the page prints no band.
beyond_lecture: Questions 7 to 10 (toxic drug level, dose-response, similar reaction on previous exposure, objective evidence) were not read out in class; each scores Yes +1, No 0.
Question 5 (alternative causes or drugs; Yes -1, No +2) was not read out, although she spoke about telling a drug cause apart from a new or changed disease state.
The numeric cut-offs (9, 5-8, 1-4, 0) were not stated aloud; she named the categories only, and said 'remote' where the page prints 'doubtful'.
The 'Do not know' column (0 points on every question) was not mentioned; she said the questions are scored yes or no.
The page prints no category for totals above 9 or below 0, which the point values allow.

terms.chapter_definition: A ten-question questionnaire 'to assess the adverse drug reaction': the user answers each question and gives the pertinent score, then totals the points.
What the total score expresses: how likely it is that the suspected drug caused the reaction, from definite down to doubtful (Total Score line).
The third answer column, worth 0 points on every one of the ten questions, so missing information neither helps nor hurts the case against the drug.
Answers that count against the drug: No on questions 2 and 4 scores -1; Yes on questions 5 and 6 scores -1.
A drug that reverses the suspected drug's effect; question 3 gives +1 if the reaction improved when the drug was stopped or a specific antagonist was given.
Giving the suspected drug again; question 4 gives +2 if the reaction reappeared and -1 if it did not.
An inactive substitute; question 6 gives -1 if the reaction reappeared when a placebo was given and +1 if it did not.
Measurable confirmation of the event, such as a test result; question 10 gives +1 if the adverse event was confirmed by any objective evidence.
Total Score 0 (her word for this band: remote).

listen: This reading is the Naranjo Algorithm, a one page questionnaire of ten questions. It matters for Exam four because Dr. Smith's study list says, "Be able to use the Naranjo algorithm." She showed it on October twenty eighth, in the lecture on adverse drug events. It scores how likely it is that one drug caused a patient's adverse reaction. Dr. Smith said, "we have to try to prove the causality to know what drug might be causing the problem." She said the answers come from sitting with the patient and asking when the drugs and the symptoms started, and what other medications they take. Each question is answered yes, no, or do not know, and each answer has set points. Do not know scores zero on every question. Dr. Smith said the questions are scored "with a yes or no," and she did not mention the do not know column. Question one asks whether there are previous conclusive reports on this reaction. Yes is plus one. She said this one is answered from the literature. Question two asks whether the adverse event appeared after the suspected drug was administered. Yes is plus two, and no is minus one. Question three asks whether the reaction improved when the drug was stopped or a specific antagonist was given. Yes is plus one. Question four asks whether the reaction reappeared when the drug was given again. Yes is plus two, and no is minus one. Question five asks whether other causes or drugs could on their own have caused the reaction. Yes is minus one, and no is plus two. Question six asks whether the reaction reappeared when a placebo was given. Yes is minus one, and no is plus one. Questions seven to ten each give plus one for yes. They ask about a toxic drug level in the blood or other fluids, a reaction that changed with the dose, a similar reaction on a previous exposure, and objective evidence. Dr. Smith pointed to questions two, three, and four as timing questions, and she counted question six as time related too. She said, "we have to think about the timing, the relationship of when they were put on this drug and when they started seeing the symptoms." She also said, "sometimes a yes is two points, sometimes it's one point, sometimes a no is negative." The points are added. The page prints four bands. A total of nine is definite, five to eight is probable, one to four is possible, and zero is doubtful. Dr. Smith said the rankings are "definite, probable, possible, or remote," so her word for the lowest band is remote. A total above nine or below zero is possible, and the page prints no band for it.
